analysis.one_liner: Taxes investment managers' carried-interest pay as ordinary income instead of at the lower capital-gains rate.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Fund managers at private equity, hedge fund, and real estate partnerships are largely paid with a share of the profits, called carried interest. Current rules let that pay be taxed at the roughly 15% capital-gains rate instead of ordinary income rates up to 35%. This bill would treat that pay as ordinary income, apply payroll taxes to it, and raise the penalty to 40% for underpaying taxes on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers in general, because the revenue now raised from lower capital-gains rates on managers' pay would no longer be lost. Fund investors' own capital gains would remain untouched — only the manager's service income changes.

how_it_helps.text: Treats the net capital gain from an 'investment services partnership interest' — the share of profits paid to managers who advise, manage, or arrange financing for investment assets — as ordinary income rather than capital gain [S2][S3].
Includes income from these partnership interests in self-employment earnings, so it is subject to Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes like wage income [S2][S3].

Raises the penalty for underpaying tax on this income from 20% to 40%, and prevents such income from qualifying for other preferences like the public-partnership and small-business-stock breaks [S2][S3].
Exempts genuine invested capital: a manager's own 'qualified capital interest' — money actually contributed — keeps capital-gains treatment; only pay for services is recharacterized [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Fund managers at private equity, hedge fund, venture capital, and real estate partnerships, who would pay ordinary income rates (up to 35% at the time) plus payroll taxes on their performance-based pay.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private equity and hedge fund managers

drawbacks.text: Critics argue taxing performance-based pay at ordinary rates penalizes risk-taking and could reduce investment in businesses, though the bill carefully preserves capital-gains treatment for managers' own invested money [S3].

Real estate held for rental or investment is covered, so real estate partnerships and developers that use carried-interest pay would face higher taxes, a cost that could affect development activity [S3].

The rules are complex — defining when an interest is pay for services versus genuine capital requires detailed allocation, valuation, and anti-abuse rules, raising compliance costs and the risk of avoidance disputes [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change is targeted: it ends a rate difference that benefits a small group of very high earners whose pay comes from managing other people's money, while leaving their genuine invested capital taxed as capital gains. The main honest costs are higher taxes on real estate and investment partnerships and added compliance complexity, but the revenue and fairness gains fall on a narrow, wealthy population.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the same day, and the committee never acted on it, so it died when the 112th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sander Levin introduced the Carried Interest Fairness Act on February 14, 2012, joined by Charles Rangel, with one cosponsor in total [S1][S4][S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means on the day of introduction [S1][S5].
No further action was recorded — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — and the bill expired when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fund managers at private equity, hedge fund, and real estate partnerships are better off, since the carried-interest tax break survived the 112th Congress untouched.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fund managers keeping their tax break

for.name: Sander Levin
for.role: U.S. Representative (D-MI), bill sponsor and senior Ways and Means member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its companion tax language, framing carried interest as service income to be taxed as ordinary income

for.name: Charles Rangel
for.role: U.S. Representative (D-NY), original cosponsor and former Ways and Means chairman
for.what_they_did: Joined Levin as the bill's only cosponsor at introduction

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill after it was referred; it died in committee

against.name: Private equity and hedge fund industry
against.role: Investment partnerships whose managers' pay depends on carried interest
against.what_they_did: Opposed carried-interest tax increases during this era through one of Washington's best-funded lobbying campaigns, publicly defended the capital-gains treatment as rewarding risk-taking

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the sponsor and its single cosponsor were both Democrats, and the Republican-controlled committee and House took no action on it.

industries.industry: Private equity and hedge fund managers
industries.note: Their performance-based pay would be taxed at ordinary rates up to 35% plus payroll taxes instead of the roughly 15% capital-gains rate, ending a preference worth billions annually. They fought similar bills throughout this period and the preference survived.
Real estate held for rental or investment is a 'specified asset,' so real estate carried-interest pay would also be taxed as ordinary income, raising costs for a heavily leveraged industry.
The bill would recapture revenue currently lost to the capital-gains rate on managers' service pay and add payroll-tax contributions, reducing the tax burden shifted onto other taxpayers.
